notes.b: Chemistry measurements only make sense when everyone uses the same units. SI (the international system of units) gives one agreed set, and you often have to convert between it and the smaller units used in the lab.
points: The SI base units used in chemistry are the metre (m) for length, kilogram (kg) for mass, second (s) for time, kelvin (K) for temperature and mole (mol) for amount of substance. Derived units are built from these, such as m³ for volume and the pascal (Pa) for pressure.
Volume: 1 dm³ (a cubic decimetre, a cube 10 cm along each edge) = 1 L = 1000 cm³ = 1000 mL. Also 1 m³ = 1000 dm³ = 1 000 000 cm³.
Mass: 1 kg = 1000 g, and 1 g = 1000 mg (milligrams), so a quantity in grams is turned into milligrams by multiplying by 1000.

Temperature: T (K) = θ (°C) + 273.15, often rounded to 273, where θ is the Celsius temperature. For example 25 °C = 298 K. Use kelvin in gas calculations because the kelvin scale starts at 0 K, with no negative values.

Pressure: 1 kPa = 1000 Pa. The IUPAC (the international chemistry organisation) standard pressure is 100 kPa (1 × 10⁵ Pa), and 1 atm (one atmosphere, the average air pressure at sea level) = 101 325 Pa.
Convert by multiplying or dividing by the conversion factor (the number linking the two units) and writing the unit at each step, so mistakes show up. For example 250 cm³ = 250 ÷ 1000 = 0.250 L.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to convert units: cm³ to L, °C to K and g to mg. Write the unit at every step of the conversion.

notes.b: Two words that sound alike describe how good a measurement is: accuracy and precision. They mean different things, and every instrument also has limits on how well it can measure.
points: Accuracy is how close a measurement, or a mean (the average of repeated readings), is to the true or accepted value.
Precision is how close repeated measurements are to each other, meaning their spread.
Precision is also used for the smallest division an instrument can read, which is its resolution. A scale marked in 0.1 cm³ steps has a finer resolution than one marked in 1 cm³ steps.
Results can be precise but not accurate, such as closely grouped readings that are all off the true value because a balance has not been zeroed (set to read 0 g with nothing on it).
Results can be accurate on average but not precise, with readings scattered on either side of the true value so that the mean lands close to it.

Every instrument has an uncertainty, the amount by which a reading could be out. Typical school values are ±0.06 cm³ for a 25 cm³ pipette, ±0.05 cm³ per reading for a 50 cm³ burette, ±0.3 cm³ for a 250 cm³ volumetric flask and about ±1 cm³ for a 100 cm³ measuring cylinder.

Volumetric glassware (pipettes, burettes and volumetric flasks, made to deliver or hold one exact volume) is far more accurate than a measuring cylinder, which is why a pipette is used for accurate volumes.

Significant figures (assumed knowledge): answers are reported to the same number of significant figures (the meaningful digits in a number) as the least precise measurement used, so the answer does not look more exact than the data. This is usually three in titration calculations.
notes.tip: Precise does not mean accurate, so keep the two definitions separate. If asked why a pipette is used rather than a measuring cylinder, say that volumetric glassware is far more accurate.

notes.b: No measurement is perfect. Errors fall into two types that behave differently, and knowing which type you have tells you how to reduce it.
points: Random error is unpredictable variation that scatters readings above and below the true value. Examples are misjudging the end point of a titration (the moment the indicator changes colour), reading a meniscus (the curved surface of a liquid in glassware) and temperature fluctuations. It is reduced by repeating and averaging, because the highs and lows cancel out.

Systematic error is a consistent error that shifts all readings in the same direction. Examples are a balance that has not been zeroed, a thermometer that reads 1 °C high, heat lost to the surroundings in a calorimetry experiment (one that measures heat changes), and parallax always from the same angle.

Repeating does not reduce systematic error, because every repeat is wrong in the same way. It is reduced by calibrating the equipment (checking it against a known standard and adjusting it) or by improving the method.
Parallax error occurs when a scale is read from an angle, which makes the liquid level appear to sit at a different mark. Read the bottom of the meniscus at eye level.
Anomalous results (outliers, readings that do not fit the rest) caused by mistakes are identified and either repeated or excluded with a reason.
Percentage error = (experimental value − accepted value) ÷ accepted value × 100.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to distinguish random and systematic error with examples. Repeating reduces random error only, so systematic error needs a better method or calibration. For a titration, end-point judgement is a random error, while a burette not rinsed with solution, or always reading the top of the meniscus, is a systematic one.

notes.b: Data are the observations and measurements collected in an experiment. They come in two kinds, and you choose which to record according to what the question asks.
points: Qualitative data are descriptions without numbers, such as a colour change, effervescence (fizzing as a gas is given off) or a precipitate (an insoluble solid) forming.
Quantitative data are measurements with numbers and units, such as a mass in g or a volume in cm³.
Select the data that answer the question. Record the raw data (the readings exactly as measured) first, then the processed data, such as means and rates, which are worked out from the raw data.
notes.tip: Record raw data before you process it, so the original readings are still there to check.

notes.b: A results table organises raw data so it can be read and graphed. A set layout means a reader can see at once what was changed and what was measured.
points: The independent variable (the quantity you change) goes in the first column. The dependent variable (the quantity you measure in response) and its repeats go in the following columns, with a mean column.
Each column heading gives the quantity and its unit, e.g. “Time / s”, so units are not written in the body of the table.
All readings are recorded to the same number of decimal places, matching the resolution of the instrument (the smallest division it can read).

notes.b: A graph turns a table of results into a picture of the pattern, and it lets you read off values or find a rate.
points: The independent variable is plotted on the x-axis (horizontal) and the dependent variable on the y-axis (vertical). Both axes are labelled with the quantity and its unit.
Scales are chosen so that the points fill more than half of the grid, with even and sensible intervals.
Points are plotted accurately as small crosses, which show the exact position of each reading.
A line or smooth curve of best fit is drawn through the general trend, because the line shows the underlying pattern. The points are not joined dot to dot.
The line is not forced through the origin unless the origin is a real data point.
A line graph is used when both variables are continuous (can take any value in a range, such as time and volume); a bar chart is used for categories.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to plot a graph from a table of results and use it to read off a value or find a rate. Plot the points, draw a line or curve of best fit through the general trend, and do not join point to point.

notes.b: Once the data are plotted, you describe the pattern, measure it and use it to predict. These skills are used to read off values, find rates and draw conclusions.
points: Describe the pattern: the values increase, decrease, level off, are directly proportional (a straight line through the origin, so doubling one variable doubles the other) or are inversely proportional (one variable goes up as the other goes down).
The gradient (steepness) of a straight line is the change in y divided by the change in x.
For a curve, the gradient at a point is found from a tangent (a straight line touching the curve at that point only) drawn at that point; this gives a rate.
Interpolation reads a value within the range of the data; extrapolation extends the line beyond it and is less reliable, because the pattern may not continue outside the range measured.
Both interpolation and extrapolation are predictions.
Trends in a table or a series of compounds allow predictions, e.g. the boiling point of the next alkane (the next hydrocarbon in the series) can be predicted from the trend in the series.

Mathematical representations (equations linking quantities) are rearranged and used, e.g. PV = nRT, the gas equation linking pressure, volume, amount in moles and temperature. Means, percentages and rates are calculated.
notes.tip: To find a rate from a graph, draw a tangent at the time asked for and take its gradient, giving the answer with units, e.g. cm³ s⁻¹ for gas volume against time.

notes.b: Chemistry uses very large and very small numbers, such as the number of particles in a mole. Scientific notation writes them compactly.
points: Scientific notation (standard form) writes a number as A × 10ⁿ, where A is between 1 and 10 and n is a whole number (the power of ten).
The Avogadro constant (the number of particles in one mole) is 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
0.00050 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴: the decimal point moves four places to the right, so the power of ten is −4.

notes.b: The last steps of analysis are to deal with any result that does not fit and then to state what the data show. A good conclusion is tied to the data and to the hypothesis (the prediction being tested).
points: An anomalous result does not fit the pattern of the other results. It is identified on the graph or in the table, and a reason is suggested, such as a misreading.
An anomalous result is left out of the mean and of the line of best fit, and this is stated, so the reader knows the data were treated openly.
A conclusion states the relationship shown by the data and says whether it supports the hypothesis.
A conclusion explains the relationship using scientific theory or a model, e.g. collision theory (the model that reactions happen when particles collide).
The conclusion is justified by reference to the data and states its limits: the range tested, the amount of data and the size of the errors.
Correlation (a link between two variables) does not prove causation (that one causes the other): the link may be due to a third factor.
notes.tip: A mean is calculated without anomalous results. Exams ask you to identify an anomalous result and explain how to treat it, and to draw a conclusion and relate it to the hypothesis.

keyTerms.definition: The internationally agreed system of units, with base units including the metre, kilogram, second, kelvin and mole.
How close a measurement, or a mean, is to the true or accepted value.
How close repeated measurements are to each other.
The smallest division that an instrument can read.
Unpredictable variation that scatters readings above and below the true value, reduced by repeating and averaging.
A consistent error that shifts all readings in the same direction, which is not reduced by repeating.
An error caused by reading a scale from an angle rather than at eye level.
The difference between the experimental and accepted values, divided by the accepted value and multiplied by 100.
The digits in a number that are meaningful, used to match the precision of an answer to the measurements used.
A result that does not fit the pattern of the other results.
Descriptions of observations that do not involve numbers.
Measurements recorded as numbers with units.
For a straight line, the change in y divided by the change in x; for a curve, the gradient of the tangent at a point.
A straight line or smooth curve drawn through the general trend of plotted points, not joining them point to point.
Estimating a value within the range of the data from a graph.
Estimating a value beyond the range of the data by extending a graph, which is less reliable.
Describes two variables whose graph is a straight line through the origin, so that one doubles when the other doubles.
A way of writing a number as A × 10ⁿ, where A is between 1 and 10.
A relationship between two variables in which one tends to change with the other.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between random error and systematic error, giving one example of each from a titration.
questions.model: Random error is unpredictable variation that scatters the readings above and below the true value, for example misjudging the colour change at the end point; repeating and averaging reduces it. Systematic error is a consistent error that shifts every reading in the same direction, for example a burette that has not been rinsed with the titrant, so the solution is diluted, or always reading the top of the meniscus; repeating does not remove it, but calibrating the equipment or improving the method does.

questions.prompt: Convert (i) 37 °C to kelvin, (ii) 0.150 L to cm³, (iii) 2.5 g to mg, (iv) 250 kPa to Pa.
A student measured the volume of gas produced every 30 s in a reaction. Describe how she should draw a graph of the results and how she could use the graph to find the rate of reaction at 60 s.
questions.model: Volume of gas is plotted on the y-axis and time on the x-axis, with both axes labelled with the quantity and unit, for example cm³ and s. The scales are chosen so that the points fill more than half of the grid, the points are plotted as small crosses, and a smooth curve of best fit is drawn through the general trend, not joining the points dot to dot. Any anomalous result is identified, left out of the line of best fit, and this is stated. To find the rate at 60 s, a tangent is drawn to the curve at the point where time is 60 s, and its gradient is calculated as the change in volume divided by the change in time, giving the rate with units of cm³ s⁻¹.
